title: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) for Intent-to-Configuration NetOps: Null Results on a Synthetic Verifier-Checked Task Bank
abstract: We ran a preregistered, fully archived paired experiment to test whether inserting a deterministic verifier plus a bounded LLM-guided repair loop (Generate–Verify–Repair, GVR) reduces verifier-detected semantic invariant violations when translating operator intents to device configurations. Using a public synthetic NetOps task bank (N = 240 paired tasks), a pybatfish-style deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), and gpt-5-mini as the generator, we executed the preregistered paired confirmatory comparison of (A) an unconstrained baseline and (C) the GVR intervention under shared-initial-candidate semantics (one initial generation reused across arms; one bounded repair allowed). All 240 pairs completed without infra/model failures. Every candidate passed the deterministic validator in both arms (n11 = 240; n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). The paired estimate (rate_C − rate_A) = 0.0, exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00, paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed 1729). Repair was not applied for any episode because the shared initial candidate already satisfied verifier predicates. The preregistration included a second prespecified comparison versus a schema-constrained baseline; that second adapter-configured comparison was not executed in the archived run (see Methods and Disclosure). We analyze why GVR produced a null confirmatory result in this setting (shared-generation semantics and task/verifier characteristics), report exact execution/accounting facts from the archived manifests, and discuss implications and reproducible next steps (adversarial tasks, multiple generators, stronger semantic or formal verifiers) needed to evaluate operational reliability of agentic NetOps pipelines.

sections.introduction: Intent-driven automation for network configuration is a promising NetOps use case for large language models (LLMs) and agentic toolchains, but operational adoption requires reliable, verifiable correctness. Prior work documents frequent LLM failures (hallucination, fabricated identifiers, incorrect code/tool calls) and proposes architectures that interpose deterministic validators and bounded repair loops (Generate–Verify–Repair, GVR) to reduce mechanically checkable defects. We preregistered a confirmatory paired experiment to evaluate: Does a deterministic verifier plus a bounded LLM-guided repair loop reduce verifier-detected semantic invariant violations compared to a strong unconstrained baseline when translating natural-language intents into device configurations? Our contributions are: (1) a machine-readable preregistration and an archived autonomous execution of a paired experiment on a public synthetic NetOps task bank (N=240 pairs); (2) an exact confirmatory paired analysis using a pybatfish-style deterministic validator and gpt-5-mini; and (3) a diagnostic interpretation that reconciles experimental design choices (notably shared-initial-candidate semantics) with the observed null result and a concrete, reproducible agenda for more sensitive follow-up evaluations.
sections.related_work: LLM hallucinations and generation failures in code and tool-calling contexts are well documented and motivate validator-inserted architectures [Cadenas 2026; Zhang et al. 2025; Huang et al. 2026]. Generate–Verify–Repair and related generate–validate–repair patterns have improved mechanically checkable outcomes (compilation, tests) in prior studies, but domain-level semantic guarantees remain an open challenge [Cadenas 2026; Yang et al. 2026]. Grammar/schema-constrained decoding improves syntactic and executable output rates but does not by itself guarantee semantic correctness for network-policy or reachability invariants [ChemRxiv 2026; Schmidt & Cimiano 2024]. Several NetOps prototypes and frameworks emphasize validators and human oversight, but controlled preregistered paired tests of GVR versus strong baselines are scarce, leaving open questions about when and how GVR materially reduces semantic violations in realistic NetOps workloads [Wang et al. 2024; Zhou et al. 2025]. Our experiment targets that evidence gap with an explicit preregistered estimand and archived execution artifacts.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: We froze a preregistration (study_id c1_gvr_semantic_eval_prereg_v1) prior to execution. The public synthetic NetOps task bank comprised 12 topology/policy clusters × 20 tasks = 240 tasks; each task includes an initial device state, a natural-language intent, explicit workflow/safety constraints, and an expected final state. The primary estimand was the paired difference in verifier-detected semantic-violation rate (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). Two primary comparisons were prespecified in the preregistration (C vs A and C vs B) with Bonferroni correction (family alpha = 0.05 → per-comparison alpha = 0.025). Execution contract and generation semantics: the registered adapter (hosted_netops_gvr_v1) executed a paired design with generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate and independent_condition_generation = false; i.e., a single initial generation was produced per task and reused for scoring in both arms, and the GVR arm was permitted one bounded repair attempt. The preregistered execution budget allowed at most one initial generation and at most one repair call per task (maximum_model_calls = 480 across all planned episodes). The generator requested was gpt-5-mini and the deterministic oracle was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (pybatfish-style diagnostics: reachability matrices, ACL-violation lists, counterexample flows). Repair policy: a single bounded repair iteration with an explicit edit budget (documented in the preregistration) was allowed; repairs exceeding the edit budget would be flagged and counted as unsuccessful repairs in sensitivity analyses. Analysis plan: the archived analysis executor paired_binary_analysis_v1 implemented an exact McNemar-style two-sided test for the paired estimand, computed absolute risk reduction and paired-bootstrap 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729), and ran preregistered sensitivity analyses for infrastructure failures. Reproducibility and verification: execution and analysis artifacts (execution manifest, deterministic reconciliation, raw responses, validator traces, and analysis CSVs) were archived before manuscript drafting and are authoritative for all reported numerical values. Important preregistration fidelity note: the preregistration included two prespecified primary comparisons (C vs A and C vs B). The archived run executed the adapter-configured paired experiment comparing the unconstrained baseline (A) to the guarded GVR condition (C) under shared-initial-candidate semantics. The prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison (C vs B) was not executed in the archived run; this absence is recorded in the archived analysis artifacts and is reported below as a limitation (the artifacts do not record a rationale for that omission).
sections.results: Execution accounting and manifest facts (archived): planned_episode_count = 480 (240 tasks × 2 scored conditions), completed_episode_count = 480, complete_pair_count = 240, model_calls_used = 240. The apparent half-count of model calls versus episodes is explained by the shared-initial-candidate design: one initial generation per task produced a candidate that was scored in both conditions, so one model call produced the candidate used by both arms and the GVR repair stage was available but not applied in these episodes. Confirmatory outcome (archived analysis): all 240 task pairs completed without infrastructure or model-call failures; validator-scored outcomes were negative for verifier-detected semantic violations for every generated candidate in both baseline and guarded conditions. Contingency counts: n11 = 240 (both accepted), n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Paired estimate: rate_guarded − rate_baseline = 0.0. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00. Paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap resamples = 10,000; seed = 1729). Repair application: repair_applied = false for all episodes because the shared initial candidate already satisfied validator predicates in every task; therefore no repair-produced artifacts changed final configurations. Missingness and exclusions: complete_pairs = 240; failed episodes = 0; no exclusions were applied. Deterministic reconciliation: archived deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms episode accounting consistency (baseline_success_count = 240; guarded_success_count = 240; provider_call_audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 240 and stage_counts = {"shared_initial_generation": 240}), corroborating the shared-generation explanation above. Secondary analyses and sensitivity checks archived in the analysis artifacts (cluster stratifications, contamination checks, conservative failure-as-violation sensitivity) do not alter the primary null outcome.
sections.discussion: Summary interpretation: In this preregistered synthetic evaluation, GVR did not reduce verifier-detected semantic violations because the generator (gpt-5-mini) produced verifier-compliant configurations on the initial shared candidate for every task; consequently the repair stage was never applied. Two non-exclusive, artifact-backed explanations account for the null confirmatory result: (1) the synthetic task bank plus the deterministic validator defined predicates that the generator (with the supplied prompting and schema constraints) could satisfy reliably on this distribution, making repair unnecessary; (2) the shared-initial-candidate design substantially reduces opportunities for different per-condition generator outputs, limiting contrasts that would expose GVR benefits when initial candidates differ across arms. Design implications: the shared-generation semantics (one model call reused across arms) is an explicit, preregistered design choice (documented in the execution_contract) that lowered model-call cost and guaranteed comparability of scoring inputs, but it also reduces sensitivity for interventions that rely on independent stochastic variation between arms. Preregistration fidelity: the preregistration specified two prespecified primary comparisons (C vs A and C vs B). The archived run executed the adapter-configured paired experiment comparing unconstrained baseline (A) versus guarded GVR (C) only; the prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison (C vs B) was not executed and the run artifacts do not contain a recorded rationale for that omission—this absence is stated here as an unresolved procedural limitation. Operational implications: a GVR pipeline can be redundant on task distributions where generator+prompting already satisfy verifier predicates, but such redundancy should not be generalized without adversarial and cross-model evaluation because (a) passing a deterministic verifier does not guarantee absence of all operational risks (oracle incompleteness), and (b) single-model dependence and synthetic-task external validity limit generality. Recommendations grounded in archived artifacts: (i) run follow-up evaluations that remove shared-generation semantics (independent per-condition generation) so per-condition generator variability can be observed; (ii) inject adversarial, vendor-diverse, and out-of-distribution tasks designed to trigger semantic violations beyond current verifier predicates; (iii) evaluate multiple generator families and stronger semantic/formal verifiers (SMT or constraint-hybrid oracles) to measure cross-model robustness and oracle coverage; (iv) measure repair utilization and human-in-the-loop costs when repair is invoked. These steps are consistent with the planned outputs and unresolved questions recorded in the preregistration and archived analysis artifacts.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, archived paired experiment testing GVR on a synthetic intent-to-configuration NetOps task bank. Under shared-initial-candidate semantics, every initial generated candidate passed the deterministic validator in both baseline and guarded arms (n = 240 pairs), yielding a null confirmatory result: GVR did not reduce verifier-detected semantic-violation rates in this run (paired estimate 0.0; McNemar p = 1.00; 95% CI [0.0, 0.0]). The execution and analysis artifacts are archived and authoritative for the reported numbers. The result demonstrates that (a) when generator+prompting already meet verifier predicates, GVR may be redundant on that distribution, and (b) rigorous, adversarial, cross-model, and independent-generation experiments with stronger semantic or formal oracles are needed before asserting operational reliability of agentic NetOps pipelines.

limitations: Synthetic task bank and verifier scope: N = 240 tasks were synthetic and evaluated against a pybatfish-style deterministic validator; results may not generalize to production topologies, vendor-specific syntax, or semantic invariants not encoded in the verifier.

Shared-generation semantics: the archived run used generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate (one initial generation per task reused across arms). This design reduced model-call cost but also reduced sensitivity to interventions that depend on independent per-condition generator variability, limiting the ability of GVR to demonstrate benefit in this run.
Single-model evaluation: the experiment used one generator (gpt-5-mini); cross-model generality is not established.
Repair budget: only a single bounded repair iteration was permitted; different or larger repair budgets or iterative strategies might produce different outcomes.
Verifier completeness risk: passing the deterministic verifier does not guarantee absence of all operational risks (unobserved invariants or properties outside the verifier model).

Prespecified comparison not executed: the preregistration included a prespecified schema-constrained-baseline comparison (C vs B) that was not executed in the archived run; the artifacts do not record a rationale, which is an unresolved procedural limitation.
